the-project-proposition.text: Proofs let data provision become a computational business while terminals keep trust policy. Ordinary capacity can scale through caches and replicas. Interoperability and practical switching are acceptance targets; the decision record owns the evidence boundary.

two-attractive-trust-deals.text: An own anchor offers the optimal deal for trust independence. Institutional publications offer an exceptionally attractive operational deal with explicit trust. Both retain software and cryptographic assumptions. Anchors sharing engines, nodes or infrastructure can fail together; agreement is not implementation diversity. The diagram separates root selection from service purchase and combines roots and evidence at terminal verification.

what-applications-buy.text: Application operators buy generic ledger services and may separately buy application interpretation and proofs. Availability agreements specify coverage, chainpoint retention, session leases, capacity, latency, uptime, recovery, prices and accounting. Each dimension needs observable behavior. Commercial promises govern delivery; a proof cannot make an unavailable provider answer. Rollback, billing and remedies remain open contracts.

switching-must-preserve-verification.text: A replacement provider serves the same network, chainpoint, commitment scheme and claims under a new local session. If it cannot serve the view or history, it reports the limitation. Switching must preserve anchor policy and proof strength. Acceptance must demonstrate equivalent verified claims across providers and rejection of altered data or substituted roots.

design-decisions.text: Separate trust choice from purchased capacity. Offer both independent anchors and institutional publications. Price observable availability instead of treating proofs as uptime guarantees. Require switching evidence instead of assuming an API creates a competitive market.

evidence-and-next-step.text: Follow the decision record for evidence limits. Next specify service and proof contracts, measure anchor and provider costs separately and demonstrate switching.
